claim: PEDF was first identified as a neurotrophic factor.
source: It was first identified as a neurotrophic factor and later as the most potent natural antiangiogenic factor, a stem cell niche factor, and an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about PEDF's discovery history.

claim: PEDF is the most potent natural antiangiogenic factor.
source: It was first identified as a neurotrophic factor and later as the most potent natural antiangiogenic factor, a stem cell niche factor, and an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: PEDF is a stem cell niche factor.
source: It was first identified as a neurotrophic factor and later as the most potent natural antiangiogenic factor, a stem cell niche factor, and an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: PEDF is an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
source: It was first identified as a neurotrophic factor and later as the most potent natural antiangiogenic factor, a stem cell niche factor, and an inhibitor of cancer cell growth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by extensive citations in the introduction.

claim: PEDF has therapeutic value in treating blinding diseases and diverse cancer types as demonstrated by numerous animal models.
source: Numerous animal models demonstrated its therapeutic value in treating blinding diseases and diverse cancer types.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the introduction.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 are cell-surface receptors for PEDF.
source: Here we report the identification of transmembrane proteins PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 as cell-surface receptors for PEDF.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including binding assays, loss of function, and gain of function studies.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 have cell type-specific receptor activities.
source: Using distinct cellular models, we demonstrate their cell type-specific receptor activities through loss of function and gain of function studies.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments in three different cell types (RAW267.4, SVEC4-10, and 661W) showing differential dependence on PLXDC1 vs PLXDC2.

claim: PEDF receptors form homooligomers under basal conditions.
source: Our experiments suggest that PEDF receptors form homooligomers under basal conditions, and PEDF dissociates the homooligomer to activate the receptors.
evidence: This is supported by copurification experiments, copper phenanthroline crosslinking, and FRET analysis.

claim: PEDF dissociates the receptor homooligomer to activate the receptors.
source: Our experiments suggest that PEDF receptors form homooligomers under basal conditions, and PEDF dissociates the homooligomer to activate the receptors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper phenanthroline crosslinking showing PEDF inhibits dimer formation, live cell assays showing PEDF causes dissociation of extracellular domain, and FRET showing time-dependent decrease in FRET signal upon PEDF addition.

claim: Mutations in the intracellular domain can have profound effects on receptor activities.
source: Mutations in the intracellular domain can have profound effects on receptor activities.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Y481F mutation in PLXDC1 showing greatly enhanced PEDF response, and S506A/Y511F mutations in PLXDC2 showing enhanced cell death activity.

claim: PEDF was originally identified as EPC-1, a factor downregulated by more than 100-fold in aged compared to young human fibroblasts.
source: It was also initially known as EPC-1, a factor that is downregulated by more than 100-fold in aged compared to young human fibroblasts (Pignolo et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Pignolo et al., 1993.

claim: PEDF inhibits endothelial cell migration and angiogenesis even in the presence of strong proangiogenic factors.
source: PEDF inhibits endothelial cell migration and angiogenesis even in the presence of strong proangiogenic factors (Dawson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Dawson et al., 1999.

claim: PEDF specifically targets new vessel growth without affecting pre-existing vessels.
source: It specifically targets new vessel growth without affecting pre-existing vessels.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an established property of PEDF.

claim: PEDF has potent therapeutic effects in treating ischemia-induced retinopathy, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration.
source: In addition to treating major blinding diseases such as ischemia-induced retinopathy, diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration (Stellmach et al., 2001; Semkova et al., 2002; Miyazaki et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: PEDF inhibits the growth of melanoma, neuroblastoma, osteosarcoma, hepatoblastoma, Lewis lung carcinoma, chondrosarcoma, gastric carcinoma, glioma, Wilm's tumor, prostate cancer, and pancreatic cancer.
source: PEDF has been shown to inhibit the growth of a wide variety of cancer types including melanoma, neuroblastoma, osteosarcoma, hepatoblastoma, Lewis lung carcinoma, chondrosarcoma, gastric carcinoma, glioma, Wilm's tumor, prostate cancer, and pancreatic cancer (Doll et al., 2003; Ek et al., 2006; Fernandez-Garcia et al., 2007; Broadhead et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: PEDF is an anti-inflammatory factor.
source: In addition, PEDF has also been identified as a stem cell niche factor (Pumiglia and Temple, 2006; Ramirez-Castillejo et al., 2006; Andreu-Agullo et al., 2009; Elahy et al., 2012) and an anti-inflammatory factor (Zamiri et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: PEDF is widely expressed in many tissues such as the eye, brain, spinal cord, bone, liver, heart and lung.
source: PEDF is widely expressed in many tissues such as the eye, brain, spinal cord, bone, liver, heart and lung.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: PEDF is naturally present in the blood.
source: PEDF is also naturally present in the blood (Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: PEDF level decreases during cellular senescence and aging.
source: PEDF level was found to decrease during cellular senescence and aging (Pignolo et al., 1993; Tombran-Tink et al., 1995; Francis et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: A significant decrease in PEDF level in the eyes has been observed in patients with age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy.
source: A significant decrease in PEDF level in the eyes has been observed in patients with age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, two major blinding diseases characterized by neovascularization (Ogata et al., 2001; Spranger et al., 2001; Holekamp et al., 2002; Ogata et al., 2002; Boehm et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: PEDF levels decrease with age in human eyes.
source: PEDF levels were also found to decrease with age in human eyes (Ogata et al., 2004; Smith and Steinle, 2007; Steinle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: PEDF expression has been inversely related to metastasis in gliomas, lymphangiomas, hepatoma, melanoma, lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, and prostate cancer.
source: PEDF expression has been inversely related to metastasis in a variety of cancer types such as gliomas (Guan et al., 2003), lymphangiomas (Sidle et al., 2005), hepatoma (Matsumoto et al., 2004), melanoma (Orgaz et al., 2009), lung cancer (Zhang et al., 2006a), pancreatic cancer (Uehara et al., 2004), and prostate cancer (Halin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Expression of PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 confers extracellular PEDF binding to live cells.
source: We found that expression of PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 confers extracellular PEDF binding to live cells (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biotinylated PEDF binding assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 with a deletion of the extracellular domain no longer binds PEDF.
source: PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 with a deletion of the extracellular domain no longer binds PEDF, while deletion of the intracellular domain has no effect on PEDF binding (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PEDF binding assays shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Deletion of the intracellular domain of PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 has no effect on PEDF binding.
source: PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 with a deletion of the extracellular domain no longer binds PEDF, while deletion of the intracellular domain has no effect on PEDF binding (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PEDF binding assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PEDF binds to cell-surface transmembrane domain proteins PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 through their extracellular domains.
source: These experiments demonstrated that PEDF binds to cell-surface transmembrane domain proteins PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 through their extracellular domains.
evidence: This is concluded from the domain deletion experiments showing that extracellular domain is required for PEDF binding.

claim: Both PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 are expressed in RAW267.4, SVEC4-10, and 661W cells.
source: We found that both PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 are expressed in these three cellular models, consistent with previous knowledge that both RAW267.4 and SVEC4-10 cells express PLXDC1 (Wang et al., 2005; Gaultier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations for RAW267.4 and SVEC4-10.

claim: PEDF stimulates secretion of IL-10 in macrophage RAW267.4 cells.
source: In macrophage RAW267.4, PEDF is known to stimulate secretion of IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine (Zamiri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: Knocking down either PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 leads to a substantial decrease in PEDF response in RAW267.4 cells.
source: We found that knocking down of either PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 led to a substantial decrease in PEDF response (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transfection of either PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 into macrophages augments PEDF-induced secretion of IL-10 without increasing basal activity.
source: Conversely, transfection of either receptor into macrophages further augments PEDF-induced secretion of IL-10 without increasing basal activity (basal activity is defined as receptor activity without PEDF treatment) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PLXDC1 or PLXDC2 lacking the cytoplasmic domain does not enhance PEDF-induced IL-10 secretion in macrophages.
source: Either receptor lacking the cytoplasmic domain no longer has this activity, consistent with role of the cytoplasmic domain in cellular signaling (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with cytoplasmic domain deletion mutants shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tyrosine 481 in human PLXDC1 is a highly conserved residue in the cytoplasmic domain and is a potential phosphorylation site.
source: Tyrosine 481 in human PLXDC1 is a highly conserved residue in the cytoplasmic domain and is a potential phosphorylation site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in the alignment in Figure 2C.

claim: PLXDC1 with Y481F mutation has highly enhanced PEDF-mediated response without increasing the basal activity of the receptor.
source: PLXDC1 with a mutation of this single residue in the cytoplasmic domain (Y481F) has highly enhanced PEDF-mediated response without increasing the basal activity of the receptor (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: PLXDC1 transfected cells show about 100% increased activity in response to 2 nM PEDF compared to control cells.
source: PLXDC1 transfected cell shows about 100% increased activity in response to 2 nM PEDF as compared to control cells, while PLXDC1-Y481F cells showed about 400% increased activity in response to PEDF (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PLXDC1-Y481F cells show about 400% increased activity in response to PEDF compared to control cells.
source: PLXDC1 transfected cell shows about 100% increased activity in response to 2 nM PEDF as compared to control cells, while PLXDC1-Y481F cells showed about 400% increased activity in response to PEDF (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PEDF-mediated cell death in SVEC4-10 cells was completely suppressed by siRNA-mediated knockdown of PLXDC2.
source: We found that PEDF—mediated cell death was completely suppressed by siRNA-mediated knockdown of PLXDC2, but there was no suppression by siRNA knockdown of PLXDC1 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: siRNA knockdown of PLXDC1 does not suppress PEDF-mediated cell death in SVEC4-10 cells.
source: We found that PEDF—mediated cell death was completely suppressed by siRNA-mediated knockdown of PLXDC2, but there was no suppression by siRNA knockdown of PLXDC1 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transfection of PLXDC2 cytoplasmic domain linked to the DCC transmembrane domain is sufficient to cause cell death independently of PEDF.
source: Interestingly, transfection of PLXDC2 cytoplasmic domain linked to the DCC transmembrane domain is sufficient to cause cell death independently of PEDF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 does not cause cell death when linked to DCC transmembrane domain.
source: In contrast, the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 does not have this activity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutations in two cytoplasmic residues (S506A/Y511F) that are potential phosphorylation sites in the PLXDC2 tail enhance the effect of PLXDC2 in causing cell death.
source: We also found that mutations in two cytoplasmic residues that are potential phosphorylation sites in the PLXDC2 tail enhance the effect of PLXDC2 in causing cell death (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PLXDC2 is responsible for mediating PEDF-mediated cell death in SVEC4-10 cells, while there is no detectable role of PLXDC1.
source: These experiments demonstrated that PLXDC2 is responsible for mediating PEDF-mediated cell death in this cell type, while there is no detectable role of PLXDC1.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss of function and gain of function experiments in SVEC4-10 cells.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC2 is sufficient to trigger downstream activity.
source: In addition, the cytoplasmic domain of the PLXDC2 is sufficient to trigger downstream activity.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing that PLXDC2 cytoplasmic domain linked to DCC transmembrane domain causes cell death.

claim: PEDF treatment effectively protects 661W cells against oxidative damage.
source: We found that PEDF treatment effectively protects 661W cells against oxidative damage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Knocking down PLXDC1 in 661W cells abolishes the protective effect of PEDF.
source: Knocking down PLXDC1, but not PLXDC2, in 661W cells abolishes the protective effect of PEDF (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knocking down PLXDC2 in 661W cells does not abolish the protective effect of PEDF.
source: Knocking down PLXDC1, but not PLXDC2, in 661W cells abolishes the protective effect of PEDF (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Transfection of PLXDC1 enhances the protective effect of PEDF in 661W cells.
source: Conversely, using gain of function analysis, we showed that transfection of PLXDC1 further enhances the protective effect of PEDF and that transfection of the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 protects 661W independent of PEDF (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transfection of the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 protects 661W cells independent of PEDF.
source: Conversely, using gain of function analysis, we showed that transfection of PLXDC1 further enhances the protective effect of PEDF and that transfection of the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 protects 661W independent of PEDF (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of the receptor is responsible for triggering the intracellular events during receptor activation.
source: These experiments suggest that the cytoplasmic domain of the receptor is responsible for triggering the intracellular events during receptor activation.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that cytoplasmic domain alone can activate downstream signaling.

claim: 661W cell depends on PLXDC1 for the survival promoting effect of PEDF.
source: The dependence of 661W cell on PLXDC1 for the survival promoting effect of PEDF is in contrast to SVEC4-10's dependence on PLXDC2 to mediate the cell death effect of PEDF.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss of function and gain of function experiments in 661W cells.

claim: SVEC4-10 depends on PLXDC2 to mediate the cell death effect of PEDF.
source: The dependence of 661W cell on PLXDC1 for the survival promoting effect of PEDF is in contrast to SVEC4-10's dependence on PLXDC2 to mediate the cell death effect of PEDF.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss of function and gain of function experiments in SVEC4-10 cells.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 form homooligomers in the absence of PEDF.
source: We found that PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 form homooligomers in the absence of PEDF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by copurification experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 preferentially form homooligomers rather than heterooligomers.
source: We designed experiments to compare homooligomerization and heterooligomerization and found that PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 preferentially form homooligomers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copurification experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Domain D is an important domain for oligomerization of PLXDC1.
source: Using deletion series of the extracellular domains, we identified domain D as an important domain for oligomerization (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copurification experiments with domain deletion mutants shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The last residue in the cytoplasmic domain of both PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 is a conserved cysteine.
source: We noticed that the last residue in the cytoplasmic domain of both PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 is a conserved cysteine.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and can be observed in the sequence alignments.

claim: Copper phenanthroline promotes the formation of covalent dimers of PLXDC1 through disulfide bonds.
source: Indeed, we found that copper phenanthroline promoted the formation of covalent dimers, consistent with the close proximity of the two cysteines on the cytoplasmic domain (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper phenanthroline crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The covalent dimer formed by copper phenanthroline can be cleaved under reducing conditions.
source: This covalent dimer can be cleaved under reducing conditions (Figure 5B), consistent with its linkage through a disulfide bond catalyzed by copper phenanthroline.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 5B comparing reducing and non-reducing gels.

claim: Incubation with PEDF before copper phenanthroline treatment inhibits the formation of the dimer and promotes the formation of the monomer.
source: Interestingly, incubation with PEDF before copper phenanthroline treatment inhibited the formation of the dimer and promoted the formation of the monomer, indicating that the cytoplasmic tail is no longer in close contact with another cytoplasmic tail (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copper phenanthroline crosslinking experiments with PEDF treatment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Extracellular domain B plays an important role in binding to PEDF.
source: To pinpoint the receptor domain that interacts with PEDF, we used a deletion series of PLXDC1 to perform copurification analysis with PEDF and found that extracellular domain B plays an important role in binding to PEDF (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by copurification experiments with domain deletion mutants shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Epitope-tagged extracellular domain of PLXDC1 is associated with the cell surface through its binding to coexpressed full length untagged PLXDC1.
source: Epitope-tagged extracellular domain of PLXDC1 is associated with the cell surface through its binding to the coexpressed full length untagged PLXDC1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell staining experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Incubation of cells with PEDF causes the dissociation of the extracellular domain and the loss of the epitope tag from the cell surface.
source: Incubation of the cells with PEDF causes the dissociation of the extracellular domain and the loss of the epitope tag from the cell surface (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell staining experiments with PEDF treatment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PEDF causes a time-dependent decrease in FRET signal between PLXDC1-CFP and PLXDC1-YFP.
source: We coexpressed PLXDC1 fused to a Cyan Fluorescent Protein (CFP) and PLXDC1 fused to a yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) at the C-terminus and observed a time-dependent decrease in FRET signals after addition of PEDF, but not a control extracellular protein nidogen (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A control protein nidogen does not cause a decrease in FRET signal between PLXDC1-CFP and PLXDC1-YFP.
source: We coexpressed PLXDC1 fused to a Cyan Fluorescent Protein (CFP) and PLXDC1 fused to a yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) at the C-terminus and observed a time-dependent decrease in FRET signals after addition of PEDF, but not a control extracellular protein nidogen (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Crosslinking the cysteine residues on the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 using BMOE prevents PEDF-dependent suppression of the FRET signal.
source: To show that this decrease in FRET signal was due to receptor dissociation, we crosslinked the cysteine residues on the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 using sulfhydryl-specific crosslinker bismaleimidoethane (BMOE) before PEDF addition and found that this crosslinker prevents PEDF-dependent suppression of the FRET signal (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET experiments with BMOE crosslinking shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mutation of the cysteine to serine (C500S) in PLXDC1 prevents the blocking effect of BMOE on PEDF.
source: However, mutation of the cysteine to serine (C500S) prevents the blocking effect of BMOE on PEDF (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET experiments with C500S mutant shown in Figure 7.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 represent a receptor family of their own that has two members in human.
source: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 represent a receptor family of their own that has two members in human.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the structural and functional characterization.

claim: Both PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 receptors have cell type-specific roles.
source: Through both loss of function and gain of function studies using three distinct cellular models that respond robustly to PEDF, we showed that both receptors have the expected properties of PEDF receptors in transducing PEDF signal and have cell type-specific roles.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experiments in three different cell types.

claim: PEDF receptor dimerization functions to inhibit self-activation.
source: Our experiments suggest that these receptors form homodimers under basal conditions, and the dimerization functions to inhibit self-activation.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that receptors form dimers basally and that the cytoplasmic domain alone can activate signaling.

claim: PEDF activates its receptors through dissociation of the dimer.
source: PEDF activates its receptors through dissociation of the dimer.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by three independent experimental approaches.

claim: Without oligomerization provided by the extracellular domains, the cytoplasmic domain of the PEDF receptor is sufficient to activate downstream signaling.
source: Without oligomerization provided by the extracellular domains, the cytoplasmic domain of the PEDF receptor is sufficient to activate downstream signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experiments with cytoplasmic domain constructs.

claim: Modulating the cytoplasmic domain strongly affects receptor signaling.
source: We also showed that modulating the cytoplasmic domain strongly affects receptor signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experiments with mutations in the cytoplasmic domain.

claim: A mutation in tyrosine 481 in the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 greatly enhanced PEDF-induced and PLXDC1-dependent IL-10 secretion from macrophages.
source: For example, a mutation in a conserved tyrosine residue in the cytoplasmic domain of PLXDC1 greatly enhanced PEDF-induced and PLXDC1-dependent IL-10 secretion from macrophages.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 are homologous membrane proteins with overlapping but distinct expression patterns.
source: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 are homologous membrane proteins with overlapping but distinct expression patterns in physiological and pathological conditions, as revealed by gene and protein expression studies.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to expression studies.

claim: PLXDC1 was discovered as one of the genes enriched in many types of human tumor endothelial cells.
source: PLXDC1 (also called tumor endothelial marker 7) was discovered as one of the genes enriched in many types of human tumor endothelial cells (St Croix et al., 2000; Schwarze et al., 2005; Beaty et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2007; van Beijnum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: PLXDC1 is highly expressed in the endothelial cells of diabetic retinopathy and is highly specific to diseased blood vessels.
source: PLXDC1 was also found to be highly expressed in the endothelial cells of another human disease- diabetic retinopathy- and is highly specific to diseased blood vessels (Yamaji et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC1 is expressed on the macrophage cell surface.
source: PLXDC1 is also expressed on the macrophage cell surface (Gaultier et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC1 is downregulated by LRP-1.
source: PLXDC1 is also expressed on the macrophage cell surface (Gaultier et al., 2010) and is downregulated by LRP-1, a large membrane protein involved in endocytosis of a variety of cell surface receptors (Herz et al., 1990; Herz and Strickland, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: PLXDC2 was found as one of the genes that increase in expression during cellular senescence.
source: In contrast, PLXDC2, but not PLXDC1, was found as one of the genes that increase in expression during cellular senescence (Schwarze et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC2 is one of the E2F1 target genes repressed by serum.
source: In contrast, PLXDC2, but not PLXDC1, was found as one of the genes that increase in expression during cellular senescence (Schwarze et al., 2005), as one of the E2F1 target genes repressed by serum (Hallstrom et al., 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC2 is a gene negatively correlated with malignant cell transformation in tumors and its disturbance increases tumor volume.
source: as a gene negatively correlated with malignant cell transformation in tumors and its disturbance increases tumor volume (McMurray et al., 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC2 is a candidate axon guidance molecule.
source: and as a candidate axon guidance molecule (Leighton et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC2 is one of the markers of adult stem cells.
source: Microarray analysis also revealed PLXDC2, but not PLXDC1, as one of the markers of adult stem cells (Noh, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC2 is present on the cell surface of human pluripotent stem cells.
source: Proteomic analysis also revealed PLXDC2 on the cell surface of human pluripotent stem cells (Boheler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC2 is a mitogen for neuroprogenitors.
source: PLXDC2 is also known as a mitogen for neuroprogenitors (Miller-Delaney et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PEDF expression correlates with G0 growth arrest in fibroblasts.
source: Interestingly, expression patterns of both PEDF and PLXDC2 have been previously linked to cellular growth states. PEDF expression correlates with G0 growth arrest in fibroblasts (Pignolo et al., 1993, 2003)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: PEDF induces cell cycle arrest of glioma cells.
source: and has been demonstrated to induce cell cycle arrest of glioma cells (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 represent a new type of cell-surface receptor.
source: From a different perspective, this study identified the extracellular ligand for two membrane proteins and showed that they function as cell-surface receptors that can transduce an extracellular signal. These receptors represent a new type of cell-surface receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the novel mechanism of activation.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 oligomerize in the basal state and are activated by ligand-induced dissociation.
source: They oligomerize in the basal state and are activated by ligand-induced dissociation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 behave oppositely from many known single transmembrane domain signaling receptors that are activated by ligand-induced dimerization.
source: Mechanistically, they behave oppositely from many known single transmembrane domain signaling receptors that are activated by ligand-induced dimerization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a comparison to other receptor types.

claim: Both human PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 have several isoforms.
source: PEDF receptors have at least two mechanisms to diversify their function and regulation. First, both human PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 have several isoforms.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a mechanism for functional diversity.

claim: PEDF receptors can couple to different immediate downstream molecules.
source: Second, receptors can couple to different immediate downstream molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a mechanism for functional diversity.

claim: PEDF is naturally present in several isoforms as revealed by isoelectric focusing.
source: PEDF is naturally present in several isoforms as revealed by isoelectric focusing (Tombran-Tink et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods with a citation.

claim: Not all PEDF isoforms are equally active.
source: Not all PEDF isoforms are equally active (Duh et al., 2002; Subramanian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods with citations.

claim: More negatively charged PEDF isoforms are more biologically active.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Duh et al., 2002; Subramanian et al., 2012), we found that more negatively charged PEDF isoforms are more biologically active.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods and supported by citations and the authors' own observations.

claim: Tagging significantly diminishes the biological activity of PEDF.
source: We found that tagging significantly diminishes the biological activity of PEDF. Therefore, all biological assays were performed using untagged PEDF.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods based on the authors' observations.

claim: The negative effect of epitope tagging on PEDF is likely one of the reasons that PEDF receptors are difficult to identify.
source: The negative effect of epitope tagging on PEDF is likely one of the reasons that PEDF receptors are difficult to identify.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods as speculation based on their observations.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 share about 50% homology.
source: These two membrane proteins both have a large extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, and an intracellular domain, and share about 50% homology.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and can be observed in the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PLXDC1 is also called tumor endothelial marker 7.
source: PLXDC1 (also called tumor endothelial marker 7) was discovered as one of the genes enriched in many types of human tumor endothelial cells (St Croix et al., 2000; Schwarze et al., 2005; Beaty et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2007; van Beijnum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: 661W is a neuronal cell line derived from cone photoreceptors.
source: To assay PEDF's neurotrophic activity, we used 661W cells, a neuronal cell line derived from cone photoreceptors (Tan et al., 2004; Kanan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 are called plexin domain containing 1 and plexin domain containing 2.
source: These two membrane proteins are called plexin domain containing 1 (PLXDC1) and plexin domain containing 2 (PLXDC2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: PLXDC1 and PLXDC2 have overlapping but distinct tissue expression patterns.
source: Gene and protein expression studies have revealed overlapping but distinct tissue expression patterns of PLXDC1 (St Croix et al., 2000; Gaultier et al., 2010) and PLXDC2 (Leighton et al., 2001; McMurray et al., 2008; Miller-Delaney et al., 2011; Boheler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.
